name: Cabergoline

card.summary: A prescription dopamine agonist that lowers prolactin; well studied for prolactinomas, discussed online as an add-on to hormone regimens, with documented heart-valve concerns at high doses.
card.note: Prescription-only; ergot-derived drugs have been linked to cardiac valve disease and fibrosis, mainly at the higher doses used in Parkinson's disease.

quick.overview:
Cabergoline is an ergot-derived, long-acting dopamine D2 receptor agonist taken by mouth. Its US-labelled use is for hyperprolactinemic disorders, including those caused by pituitary adenomas, and it is generally preferred over bromocriptine for prolactinomas.

In muscle and TRT-oriented communities it is discussed as a way to manage prolactin during hormone therapy. Published trials are in prolactinomas and other pituitary conditions, not in healthy people seeking appearance changes.
quick.mechanism: It stimulates D2 receptors on prolactin-producing pituitary cells, mimicking dopamine's inhibitory signal and lowering prolactin secretion; in prolactinomas it also shrinks tumours. Its half-life is long, reported around 63 to 115 hours depending on the population.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea, headache, dizziness and constipation. Ergot-derived dopamine agonists have been associated with cardiac valve regurgitation, mainly at high Parkinson's-disease doses, and the label advises cardiovascular evaluation including echocardiography. Rare pulmonary and other fibrotic complications are reported. It is prescription-only.

lead: Cabergoline is an ergoline-derived dopamine D2 receptor agonist taken orally, sold under brand names such as Dostinex and Cabaser [1][2]. The US drug label lists its indication as hyperprolactinemic disorders, either idiopathic or due to pituitary adenomas [3].

For prolactinomas, a 2017 JAMA review states that initial therapy is generally a dopamine agonist [4]. A 1994 double-blind trial of 459 women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea compared cabergoline with bromocriptine [5]. Wikipedia reports that the drug was synthesised by Farmitalia-Carlo Erba in Milan, marketed in the Netherlands in 1992 and approved by the FDA in December 1996 [2].

Safety debates centre on cardiac valve disease. Two 2007 studies in Parkinson's disease patients found associations between pergolide and cabergoline and valve regurgitation [6][7]. Cabergoline has also been studied in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, acromegaly and Cushing's disease [8][9][10]. No published trials have examined it for appearance outcomes.

paras: Its main use is hyperprolactinemia and prolactinoma [3][4]. It is also used for lactation suppression in some countries, and in some countries for Parkinson's disease, although its use there has declined because of valvulopathy concerns [2][11]. Wikipedia lists off-label uses including counteracting SSRI-related sexual side effects and reducing ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome incidence in IVF [2].

Muscle and TRT-focused communities discuss dopamine agonists such as cabergoline for managing prolactin during hormone therapy. The wiki's sources do not include trial data for this use in healthy people.

In the 1994 comparison trial, cabergoline was tested against bromocriptine in women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea, in a double-blind design with 459 participants [5]. Grokipedia and other summaries state that prolactin normalises in the majority of microprolactinoma patients, although such figures should be read against the primary literature [1][4]. Registered trials have explored rapid dose escalation in macroprolactinomas [12], higher-dose treatment in microprolactinomas [13], and dopamine agonists for non-functioning pituitary adenomas [14].

The US label reports that most adverse events in more than 900 hyperprolactinemic patients were mild or moderate, with a dose-related effect seen only for nausea [3]. Wikipedia lists nausea, vertigo, constipation and somnolence among the commonly reported effects, with rare pleural, pulmonary and pericardial fibrosis [2].

The label's warnings advise cardiovascular evaluation, including an echocardiogram, to look for valvular disease before treatment, and say patients with detected valvular disease should not be treated [3]. A UK population-based cohort of 11,417 patients and an echocardiographic study of 155 patients with Parkinson's disease both reported increased valve regurgitation with ergot-derived agonists [6][7]. Wikipedia reports that low doses used for hyperprolactinemia were not linked to clinically significant valve disease [2].

Cabergoline is a potent D2 agonist that also binds D3, D4 and several serotonin receptors, including 5-HT2B, which has been linked to valvulopathy [2][15]. Oral bioavailability is reported at 50 to 80 percent, with hepatic metabolism and mostly faecal excretion [2].
The US label places cabergoline in Category B, with animal studies showing maternal toxicity but no teratogenic effects at the doses tested [3].

Human trials are in disease populations: hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea [5], Parkinson's disease [6][7], prolactinoma dosing [12][13], non-functioning pituitary adenomas [14], metastatic breast cancer [16], acromegaly [17], ovarian hyperstimulation in polycystic ovary syndrome [8], and Cushing's disease [9][18]. A 2006 pharmacological study used cabergoline to probe dopamine function in human cognition [19]. No studies found for appearance or physique outcomes in healthy people.

timeline.event: Marketed as Dostinex in the Netherlands [2].
Studies link ergot-derived dopamine agonists to valve regurgitation [6][7].
